title: II. The Alarm
paragraphs: Our police captain, Mihail Makarovitch Makarov, a retired lieutenant colonel, was a widower and an excellent man. He'd come to us only three years before, but had won everyone's esteem, chiefly because he "knew how to keep society together." He was never without visitors, and couldn't have gotten on without them. Someone or other was always dining with him; he never sat down to a meal without guests. He also held regular dinners for all sorts of occasions, sometimes rather surprising ones. The fare wasn't exquisite, but there was plenty of it. The fish pies were excellent, and the wine made up in quantity what it lacked in quality.

The first room guests entered was a well-appointed billiard room, hung with pictures of English racehorses in black frames — an essential decoration, as we all know, for a bachelor's billiard room. There was card-playing at his house every evening, even if only at one table. But at frequent intervals, all of our town's society, mothers and young ladies included, gathered there to dance. Though Mihail Makarovitch was a widower, he didn't live alone. His widowed daughter lived with him, along with her two unmarried daughters, grown girls who'd finished their schooling. They were pleasant to look at and lively in temperament, and though everyone knew they'd have no dowry, they drew all the fashionable young men of the town to their grandfather's house.

Mihail Makarovitch was by no means highly capable at his work, though he performed his duties no worse than most others. To put it plainly, he was a man of rather limited education. His grasp of the boundaries of his own administrative authority couldn't always be relied on. It wasn't so much that he failed to understand certain reforms enacted under the present reign, as that he made conspicuous blunders interpreting them. This wasn't from any particular lack of intelligence, but from carelessness — he was always in too much of a hurry to go into things properly.

"I have the heart of a soldier, not a civilian," he liked to say of himself. He'd never even formed a clear idea of the basic principles behind the reforms tied to the emancipation of the serfs, and had only picked it up, so to speak, year by year, building his knowledge unintentionally through practice. And yet he was himself a landowner. Pyotr Ilyitch knew for certain he'd find some of Mihail Makarovitch's regular visitors there that evening, though he didn't know which ones. As it happened, at that moment the prosecutor, and Varvinsky, our district doctor — a young man who'd only just arrived from Petersburg after taking a brilliant degree at the Academy of Medicine — were playing whist at the police captain's. Ippolit Kirillovitch, the prosecutor (he was really the deputy prosecutor, but we always called him the prosecutor), was a rather peculiar man of about thirty-five, prone to consumption, married to a stout, childless woman. He was vain and irritable, though he had a sharp mind and even a kind heart. It seemed the only real trouble with him was that he thought more highly of himself than his abilities warranted. And that kept him in a state of near-constant unease. He also had certain loftier, even artistic, inclinations — toward psychology, say, a particular interest in the human heart, a particular grasp of the criminal and his crime. He nursed a grievance on this score, believing he'd been passed over in his career, and was firmly convinced that in higher circles he wasn't properly appreciated, and that he had enemies. In his gloomier moods he even threatened to resign his post and take up criminal law as a barrister. The unexpected Karamazov case stirred him profoundly: "It was a case that might well be talked about across all of Russia." But I'm getting ahead of myself.

Nikolay Parfenovitch Nelyudov, the young investigating lawyer, who'd arrived from Petersburg only two months before, was sitting in the next room with the young ladies. People talked about it afterward, marveling that all the gentlemen should, as if on purpose, have been gathered that evening — the evening of "the crime" — at the house of the local authority. And yet it was perfectly simple, and had come about quite naturally.

Ippolit Kirillovitch's wife had had a toothache for the past two days, and he'd had to get out of the house to escape her groaning. The doctor, by his very nature, couldn't spend an evening any other way than at cards. Nikolay Parfenovitch Nelyudov had been planning for three days to drop in that evening at Mihail Makarovitch's, as if by chance, in order to slyly startle the eldest granddaughter, Olga Mihailovna, by letting her know he'd found out her secret — that it was her birthday, and that she was trying to hide it on purpose so as not to have to host a dance. He looked forward to plenty of merriment: playful jokes about her age and her fear of revealing it, about his knowing her secret and telling everyone, and so on. The charming young man was a great hand at that kind of teasing; the ladies had nicknamed him "the naughty man," and he seemed rather pleased with it. He was, however, extremely well-bred, of good family, good education, good feeling, and, though he lived a life of pleasure, his jokes were always innocent and in good taste. He was short and delicate-looking. On his slender white little fingers he always wore a number of large, glittering rings. When engaged in his official duties, he turned extraordinarily grave, as though fully conscious of his position and the sanctity of the obligations resting on him. He had a special knack for confusing murderers and other criminals from the peasant class during questioning, and if he didn't manage to win their respect, he certainly managed to leave them in awe.

Pyotr Ilyitch was simply dumbfounded when he walked into the police captain's. He saw at once that everyone already knew. They'd actually thrown down their cards; everyone was on their feet, talking. Even Nikolay Parfenovitch had left the young ladies and hurried in, looking tense and ready for action. Pyotr Ilyitch was met with the stunning news that old Fyodor Pavlovitch really had been murdered that evening, in his own house — murdered and robbed. The news had only just reached them, in the following way.

Marfa Ignatyevna, wife of old Grigory, who'd been knocked senseless near the fence, was sleeping soundly in bed and might well have slept until morning, given the draught she'd taken. But all at once she woke up, no doubt roused by a terrible epileptic scream from Smerdyakov, lying unconscious in the next room. That scream always preceded his fits, and always terrified and unsettled Marfa Ignatyevna. She could never get used to it. She jumped up and ran, half-awake, to Smerdyakov's room. But it was dark in there, and all she could hear was the sick man beginning to gasp and thrash. Marfa Ignatyevna herself let out a scream then, and was about to call her husband, but suddenly realized that when she'd gotten up, he hadn't been beside her in bed. She ran back to the bedstead and groped around with her hands, but the bed was truly empty. Then he must have gone out — but where? She ran to the steps and timidly called for him. No answer came, of course, but she caught the sound of groaning somewhere off in the dark garden. She listened. The groans came again, clearly from the garden.
"Good Lord! Just like it was with Lizaveta Smerdyastchaya!" she thought, distractedly. She crept timidly down the steps and saw that the garden gate stood open.
"He must be out there, poor dear," she thought. She went up to the gate, and all at once clearly heard Grigory calling her name — "Marfa! Marfa!" — in a weak, moaning, dreadful voice.

"Lord, keep us from harm!" Marfa Ignatyevna murmured, and ran toward the voice, and that's how she found Grigory. But she found him not by the fence where he'd been struck down, but about twenty paces off. It turned out later that he'd crawled that far after coming to, and had probably taken a long time getting there, losing consciousness several times along the way. She noticed at once that he was covered in blood, and screamed at the top of her lungs. Grigory was muttering incoherently:
"He's murdered ... murdered his father.... Why are you screaming, fool ... run ... fetch someone...."

But Marfa went on screaming, and, seeing that her master's window was open with a candle lit inside, she ran to it and began calling for Fyodor Pavlovitch. But peering in through the window, she saw a horrifying sight. Her master lay motionless on his back on the floor. His light-colored dressing gown and white shirt were soaked in blood. The candle on the table lit up, brightly, the blood and the still, dead face of Fyodor Pavlovitch. Terror-struck, Marfa fled the window, ran out of the garden, drew the bolt on the main gate, and ran headlong, by the back way, to the neighbor, Marya Kondratyevna. Both mother and daughter were asleep, but woke at Marfa's desperate, unrelenting screaming and pounding on the shutter. Marfa, shrieking and gabbling incoherently, managed to get the main fact across, and to beg for help. As it happened, Foma had returned from his travels and was staying the night with them. They roused him at once, and all three ran to the scene. On the way, Marya Kondratyevna remembered that around eight o'clock she'd heard a terrible scream from their garden — no doubt Grigory's scream of "Parricide!" when he'd grabbed Mitya's leg.

"Someone screamed out once, and then went quiet," Marya Kondratyevna explained as she ran. Reaching the spot where Grigory lay, the two women, with Foma's help, carried him to the lodge. They lit a candle and saw that Smerdyakov was no better — writhing in convulsions, his eyes fixed in a squint, foam flowing from his lips. They wet Grigory's forehead with water mixed with vinegar, and it revived him at once. He asked immediately:
"Is the master murdered?"

Then Foma and both women ran to the house, and this time saw that not just the window but the garden door too stood wide open, even though Fyodor Pavlovitch had, for the past week, locked himself in every night and wouldn't let even Grigory in on any pretext. Seeing the door open, they were afraid to go in to Fyodor Pavlovitch, "in case something happened to them afterward." And when they got back to Grigory, the old man told them to go straight to the police captain. Marya Kondratyevna ran there and raised the alarm with the whole party at the police captain's house. She arrived only five minutes ahead of Pyotr Ilyitch, so his own account came through not as mere guesswork and theory on his part, but as direct confirmation, by a witness, of the theory everyone already held about the identity of the criminal — a theory he himself had, deep down, refused to believe until that very moment.

It was decided to act at once, and decisively. The deputy police inspector of the town was directed to take four witnesses, enter Fyodor Pavlovitch's house, and open an inquiry on the spot, following the proper procedures, which I won't go into here. The district doctor, a zealous man new to his work, all but insisted on accompanying the police captain, the prosecutor, and the investigating lawyer.

I'll note briefly that Fyodor Pavlovitch was found quite dead, his skull crushed in. But with what? Most likely with the very same weapon used on Grigory. And that weapon was found almost immediately: Grigory, who was given every possible medical attention at once, described, in a weak, faltering voice, how he'd been struck down. They searched by lantern along the fence and found the brass pestle, dropped in the most conspicuous spot right on the garden path. There were no signs of disturbance in the room where Fyodor Pavlovitch lay. But by the bed, behind the screen, they picked up off the floor a large, thick envelope, inscribed: "A gift of three thousand roubles for my angel Grushenka, if she's willing to come." And below that, Fyodor Pavlovitch had added, "For my little chick." The envelope bore three seals of red sealing wax, but it had been torn open and was empty — the money was gone. They also found on the floor a strip of narrow pink ribbon, which had been used to tie the envelope shut.

One piece of Pyotr Ilyitch's testimony made a strong impression on the prosecutor and the investigating magistrate — his account of Dmitri Fyodorovitch's plan to shoot himself before daybreak, that he'd resolved on it, had spoken of it to Pyotr Ilyitch, had taken the pistols, loaded them right in front of him, written a note, put it in his pocket, and so on. When Pyotr Ilyitch, still not quite believing it, had threatened to tell someone in order to stop the suicide, Mitya had answered, grinning: "You'll be too late." So they had to hurry to Mokroe to catch the criminal before he actually shot himself.

"That's clear, that's perfectly clear!" the prosecutor repeated, in great excitement. "That's exactly the way it goes with madmen like that: 'I'll kill myself tomorrow, so I'll make merry till I die!'"
The story of how he'd bought the wine and provisions worked the prosecutor up even more.

"Do you remember the fellow who murdered a merchant named Olsufyev, gentlemen? Stole fifteen hundred, went straight off to have his hair curled, and then, without even hiding the money, carrying it almost right out in his hand the same way, went off to see the girls."

Everyone was held up, though, by the inquiry, the search, and the various formalities at Fyodor Pavlovitch's house. It all took time, so, two hours before setting off, they sent ahead to Mokroe the district police officer, Mavriky Mavrikyevitch Schmertsov, who'd arrived in town the morning before to collect his pay. He was instructed to avoid raising any alarm once he reached Mokroe, but to keep the "criminal" under steady watch until the proper authorities arrived, and also to line up witnesses for the arrest, constables, and so on. Mavriky Mavrikyevitch did exactly as told, keeping his presence secret, giving no hint of his business to anyone but his old acquaintance Trifon Borissovitch. He'd spoken to him just before Mitya, searching for the landlord in the dark, met him on the balcony, and noticed at once a change in Trifon Borissovitch's face and voice. So neither Mitya nor anyone else knew he was being watched. The pistol case had been carried off by Trifon Borissovitch and stowed somewhere fitting. It was only after four o'clock, nearly at sunrise, that all the officials — the police captain, the prosecutor, the investigating lawyer — arrived in two carriages, each drawn by three horses. The doctor stayed behind at Fyodor Pavlovitch's to perform a post-mortem the next day. But he was especially interested in the condition of the servant, Smerdyakov.

"Such violent, prolonged epileptic fits, recurring continuously for twenty-four hours, are rarely seen, and are of real scientific interest," he declared enthusiastically to his companions, who laughingly congratulated him, as they left, on his find. The prosecutor and the investigating lawyer both clearly remembered the doctor saying that Smerdyakov wouldn't survive the night.
After these lengthy, but I think necessary, explanations, we'll go back to the moment in our story where we left off.
